name: Jolof Empire and Wolof kingdoms
summary: A Wolof empire in Senegal that broke up after 1549 into kingdoms such as Cayor, Waalo and Baol; they traded with Europeans on the coast until France conquered them in the 1880s.

location.value: Northern and central Senegal, between the Senegal and Gambia rivers.

terrain.value: Flat savanna and dry grassland, with the Atlantic coast to the west.

climate.value: Sahel and savanna: a rainy season from about June to October and a long dry season.

resources.value: Millet and sorghum, cattle, horses, and later groundnuts (peanuts).

population.value: Perhaps several hundred thousand across the Wolof kingdoms.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; royal capitals moved; trading posts such as Saint-Louis and Gorée grew on the coast.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; yellow fever in the coastal towns.

migration.value: Wolof states absorbed Serer and Fulani neighbours; captives were taken away in the Atlantic slave trade.

economicBase.value: Farming millet, herding, trading horses, and later growing groundnuts for export.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with Portuguese, Dutch, French on the coast.

wealth.value: Rulers grew rich by trading captives to Europeans for horses, guns and cloth.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute from vassal kingdoms, taxes on trade with Europeans, and cloth and iron as money.

inequality.value: Royal lineages, free farmers, castes, captives.

governmentType.value: Kingdoms ruled by titled kings: the Burba of Jolof, the Damel of Kayor, the Teigne of Baol and the Brak of Waalo.

keyRulers.value: Ndiadiane Ndiaye (legendary founder); Lat Dior Diop, Damel of Kayor, who resisted the French until killed in 1886.

succession.value: Kings were chosen by councils of nobles from eligible royal lineages, often with rivalry.

institutions.value: Councils of electors, royal slave soldiers (ceddo), and Muslim clerics (marabouts).

stability.value: After the Battle of Danki (1549) Jolof lost its vassals, which became separate kingdoms.

eliteConflict.value: Wars between Kayor, Baol, Waalo and Jolof; clashes between ceddo warriors and Muslim reformers.

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry was the main force; firearms bought from Europeans spread from the 1600s.

majorWars.value: Battle of Danki (1549); wars with France.

territoryChange.value: Split into Jolof, Kayor, Baol and Waalo after 1549; conquered by France in the 1800s.

alliancesRivals.value: Traded with and fought the French at Saint-Louis (from 1659); rivals of Futa Toro and the Moors.

scienceEducation.value: Qur’anic schools run by marabouts; history kept by griots.

openness.value: Open to Atlantic trade with the Portuguese, Dutch and French.

communicationTransport.value: Horses, footpaths and river boats; the Dakar–Saint-Louis railway (1885) was built through Kayor.

languageWriting.value: Wolof, an Atlantic language of the Niger–Congo family; Arabic script (Wolofal) was used by Muslims.

artsArchitecture.value: Oral epics and praise songs of the griots, drumming (sabar), and round thatched houses.

socialStructure.value: Nobles, free people, castes (griots, smiths), captives.

sharedIdentity.value: Wolof language and customs, loyalty to the ruler, and growing Muslim identity.

dailyLife.value: Millet couscous (ceere) and porridge; compounds of round houses; markets and wrestling.

neighbours.value: Futa Toro and the Moors to the north, the Serer kingdoms of Sine and Saloum, and Mande states to the east.

ideasReligions.value: Islam spread from the court to the people; Sufi orders such as the Mourides (founded by Amadou Bamba in the 1880s) became powerful.

colonisation.value: France took Waalo (1855) under Governor Faidherbe and Kayor after Lat Dior’s death (1886).

riseSignals.value: The Jolof Empire formed around 1350, uniting Wolof states under the Burba.

peakPeriod.value: About 1450–1549, when Jolof ruled Waalo, Kayor, Baol, Sine and Saloum.

declineSignals.value: Defeat by Kayor at the Battle of Danki (1549).

outcome.value: The kingdoms became part of French Senegal (by 1886–90).

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles; population figures are estimates.
